A.title: Keep the 43 forces: name a local lead and ring-fence neighbourhood officers
A.answer: Skip the merger and keep the 43 forces. The Home Secretary sets two rules in law. First, every council area gets a named neighbourhood lead, and each force must publish that area's burglary, vehicle and phone theft outcomes every month. Second, neighbourhood officer numbers and front desks are ring-fenced; a force can't cut them to fund back-office changes. Forces cut the duplication the Home Office points to (s1) by sharing back-office services by agreement, which avoids the multi-billion start-up cost a chief constable warns mergers need (s2) and the opposition that ended the 2006 plan (s2). Inspectors check this yearly. It worked if published outcomes improve and neighbourhood numbers hold.

B.title: Residents' panels, drawn by lot, can hire and fire each Commander
B.answer: Each of the roughly 200 Commands (s1) gets a standing panel of residents drawn by lot, like jury service, instead of councillors or ministers. The panel appoints the Commander, can remove them by two-thirds vote, and sees priorities, spending and crime figures published each quarter. Day-to-day operations stay with the Commander. The Home Office writes this into the Command rules before launch, since the announcement gives no cost, officer number or timetable (s1). Simulated citizens' top choice was a named Commander answerable locally; some also said politicians should not run police day to day. It worked if every Command has a panel within a year, a removal vote has been held somewhere, and residents can name their Commander.
